name: walkthrough
title: Grammar Tooling in Python
description: Walk through the labeled blocks of the CS374 tutorial on grammar tooling in Python, from a membership checker and left-recursion detection to parse trees, derivations, and an ambiguity detector. Each step explains what one block adds and what the program prints.

steps.description: `GRAMMAR` maps each nonterminal to a list of right-hand sides. E splits into E + T or T, T splits into T * F or F, and F lists the ten digits.
`derivable` searches over sentential forms, a mix of terminals and nonterminals. It expands the leftmost nonterminal at each step and keeps a visited set so the search stays finite.
When a form holds only terminals, the checker compares it with the target and stops.

steps.question: What does the checker report for the string 2++3?

steps.description: Move to left recursion detection. A nonterminal is directly left-recursive when one of its productions starts with itself.
`find_left_recursive` walks every production and flags a nonterminal when the first symbol on the right side is that same nonterminal.
The block defines three grammars: the standard left-recursive arithmetic form, a right-recursive rewrite, and a balanced-parens grammar. `report` runs the detector on each.
The detector flags a nonterminal when a production starts with that same nonterminal, which is direct left recursion.

steps.question: Which nonterminals does the detector flag in the left-recursive arithmetic grammar?

steps.description: Move to parse trees stored as nested dicts.
`leaf` builds a node with no children, and `tree` builds a node with a label and a list of children.
`pretty` prints the tree as indented lines. Each level of depth adds two spaces, so a deeper line sits under its parent.
evaluate recurses into every child first, so the deepest operations run before the ones above them.

steps.question: What value does the correct parse tree for 2 + 3 * 4 produce?

steps.description: Move to a tracer that prints a leftmost and a rightmost derivation of the same string.
`parse` is a recursive-descent parser over the layered grammar. E handles plus, T handles times, and F handles a number or a parenthesized expression.
`derivation` expands one nonterminal per step, choosing the production the tree used. It records each form as a list of symbols.
The tracer picks the leftmost or the rightmost nonterminal, depending on which derivation it is building.

steps.question: How many steps does each derivation take?
steps.answer: 8 steps, final string: num + num * num

steps.description: Move to an ambiguity detector. A grammar is ambiguous when one string has two different parse trees.
`AMBIGUOUS` holds the naive grammar E -> E + E or id. It allows either grouping of a sum.
`gen_trees` generates every tree up to a depth limit, and `trees_for` keeps the ones whose leaves match the target.
For a two-child rule the generator builds the tree as an operator with a left child and a right child.

steps.question: What does the detector conclude for a + b + c?
steps.answer: Grammar IS ambiguous: found 2 distinct parse trees.

steps.description: Move to a side-by-side comparison of the ambiguous grammar and the layered one.
`leaf` and `node` build a tree from a small dict with an operator, a value, a left child, and a right child.
Two trees are built for 2 + 3 * 4 under the ambiguous grammar, and one under the layered grammar.
The layered grammar yields one tree for the string, and it matches the tree with the plus at the root.

steps.question: What value does the tree with the star at the root produce?

steps.description: Move to the last model: a grammar stored as Python data and checked against token lists.
`GRAMMAR` names each nonterminal with a prefix: t: marks a terminal and n: marks a nonterminal. Each value is a list of alternatives.
`parse` tries each alternative in order, and `match_alt` consumes a terminal or recurses into a nonterminal. A failed alternative restores the position so the next one can be tried.
When every symbol in an alternative matches, parse reports success and the new position.

steps.question: What does the checker print in the pass column for the first case?
